title: Evaluating General-Purpose AI with Psychometrics
author: Xiting Wang · Liming Jiang · Jose Hernandez-Orallo · David Stillwell · Luning Sun · Fang Luo · Xing Xie

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied excerpts describe multidisciplinary and cognitive approaches to AI evaluation, but they report others’ work and provide no source-level findings or argument about whether benchmark scores establish workplace suitability, how benchmarks should be governed, or which failure mechanisms undermine practical reliability.
qs: This book advocates a unified view for measuring natural and artificial intelligence by integrating research from psychometrics, comparative psychology, animal cognition, and AI evaluation.

This paper uses tools from cognitive psychology to evaluate GPT-3, demystify how this model solves different tasks, and acquire insights to make recommendations for how to improve future model iterations.

st.t: Evaluation design: Preferences differ from professional correctness
st.an: The source indicates that a cited survey covers multiple dimensions of language-model evaluation, which is broadly relevant to the cluster. However, the supplied evidence does not show that this source endorses the cluster’s distinctions among answer quality, preference and workflow success, or its requirements for diagnostic metrics, cost controls and agent attribution.
qs: This survey reviews over 200 papers on large language model evaluation, offers a sum- mary based on what, where, and how to evaluate, and discusses future opportunities.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source reports general psychometric and cognitive-psychology approaches to evaluating AI, but provides no legal-workflow evidence or position on bounded-task gains, verification, lawyer replacement, organisational complements, or competence risks. Its evaluation focus is potentially relevant but insufficient to support or challenge the cluster proposition.
qs: This book advocates a unified view for measuring natural and artificial intelligence by integrating research from psychometrics, comparative psychology, animal cognition, and AI evaluation.

This paper uses tools from cognitive psychology to evaluate GPT-3, demystify how this model solves different tasks, and acquire insights to make recommendations for how to improve future model iterations.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The excerpt only notes that a cited survey reviews more than 200 papers and organises evaluation literature around what, where and how to evaluate. It provides no substantive findings establishing whether professional task execution, reproducible scoring, automated judging or self-correction should be evaluated as the cluster proposes.
qs: This survey reviews over 200 papers on large language model evaluation, offers a sum- mary based on what, where, and how to evaluate, and discusses future opportunities.

st.t: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that benchmark scores are bounded evidence rather than proof of real-world capability. It materially develops the cluster by applying psychometric methods to distinguish reliability from validity and to diagnose inconsistency across test items, raters and datasets.
qs: For example, a high success rate of an AI system on a benchmark task may not translate into high performance in real-world applications.

It goes beyond the scope of “replicability” or “robustness” in computer science, of- fering a more comprehensive examination of different types of measurement errors, such as inconsistency of results among different test items, raters, and (sub-)datasets [42].

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s warning that benchmark performance does not establish real-world capability and materially extends its evaluation framework by proposing psychometric reliability, validity and construct-oriented assessment for general-purpose AI. Its emphasis is evaluation rather than legal workflow redesign, but it strengthens the case for cautious, context-sensitive deployment.
qs: For example, a high success rate of an AI system on a benchmark task may not translate into high performance in real-world applications.
Psychometrics has developed a systematic approach to test quality assurance, focusing on both re- liability and validity of measurement.

kp.k: Task benchmarks cannot adequately evaluate general-purpose AI
kp.d: The authors argue that predefined task benchmarks lack sufficient predictive power, explanatory power and quality assurance for versatile systems deployed on unforeseen tasks. Larger collections do not resolve this underlying limitation: BIG-Bench includes over 200 tasks, but cannot cover all situations confronting a general medical assistant. This is a methodological argument, not a new empirical demonstration of benchmark failure.
qs: For example, BIG-Bench [23] includes a collection of over 200 tasks.
The assumption that AI’s performance tested on a limited number of tasks directly reflect its performance in a practically infinite range of applicable tasks is unsubstantiated [6, 28].

kp.k: Evaluate latent constructs rather than isolated task scores
kp.d: The proposed alternative measures underlying constructs that explain performance across tasks, without assuming these constructs resemble human psychological traits. The authors explicitly adopt the behavioral-science assumption that many outputs can be organized through relatively few constructs. Their contribution is a perspective and framework rather than a validated, comprehensive AI assessment instrument.
qs: To tackle these challenges, we suggest transitioning from task-oriented evaluation to construct-oriented evaluation.
Constructs are concepts that, although not observed directly, are hypothesized to underlie a range of behaviors [13, 14].
this paper is focused on leveraging the scientific theories and techniques in psycho- metrics to help identify and measure the constructs inherent in AI systems, be they human-like or not.

kp.k: Predictive benefits remain partly an extrapolation from humans
kp.d: The authors cite longitudinal human research linking cognitive and personality constructs to academic and life outcomes to motivate AI evaluation. They propose that spatial reasoning could predict performance across navigation, rotated-shape recognition and engineering design. Their stronger medical-assistant example is hypothetical: excellence in communication, clinical reasoning and problem-solving is presented as grounds for predicting performance even in undeveloped medical practices, not as an experimentally established result.
qs: Based on latent constructs, psychometrics is capable of predicting human performance on a wide range of tasks and forecasting real-world outcomes.
Imagine an AI system that proves excellent in constructs essential for a general medical assistant, for example, effective communication, clinical reasoning, and problem-solving ability.
Without testing the system on specific tasks, we can confidently predict its performance as a general medical assistant, even in medical practices yet to be developed.

kp.k: Existing factor analysis supports explanatory capability structures
kp.d: As evidence that constructs can organize AI capabilities, the authors report Burnell et al.’s factor analysis of 29 large language models on 27 cognitive tasks. The cited study identified reasoning, comprehension and core language modeling constructs explaining a high proportion of performance variance. The document gives no numerical variance estimate and does not present this as its own experiment.
qs: For example, factor analysis reveals a consistent structure in the performance of 29 different large language models on 27 cognitive tasks, which is comprised of three constructs representing reasoning, comprehension, and core language modeling [37].
These constructs explain a high proportion of the variance in model performance and provide insights into the pattern of the capabilities across different models.

kp.k: Human psychological tests may mischaracterize AI
kp.d: The authors caution against assuming that human traits or relationships between traits and observable indicators transfer intact to AI. They cite questionnaire responses changing substantially when question order changes, and explain that smaller models may process faster without being more intelligent. Human tests therefore require reconsideration and adaptation, alongside new tests designed for AI-specific constructs.
qs: First, tests developed for humans may not be reliable or valid for AI systems, even if the systems are trained on large-scale human data.

However, when applied to AI systems, a minor change in the input that is negligible to humans (such as reversing the order of the questions) may result in a substantial change in a large language model’s response [44].
Smaller models that have fewer parameters typically process faster than larger models, but this does not necessarily mean that smaller models are more intelligent.

kp.k: Construct identification requires theory, evidence and iterative refinement
kp.d: The framework begins by identifying constructs through top-down expert theory, including Delphi methods, and bottom-up empirical approaches such as factor analysis. These can be combined. Confabulation is suggested as a possible construct for fabricated or misleading AI output, subject to operational definition and validation. AI emotional intelligence might instead concern recognizing and responding to human emotions, excluding human self-awareness requirements. Initial constructs are expected to remain partial or biased until refined through evidence.
qs: our framework includes three stages: construct identification, construct measurement, and test validation.
The construct needs to be validated to ensure that it is predictive and explanatory [52].
Newly identified constructs of AI systems are likely to be partial or biased.
With enriched knowledge derived from empirical evidence, we should expect to continuously refine the definition of the constructs and their measurements.

kp.k: Test design must isolate intended constructs
kp.d: The measurement stage requires explicit test guidelines and item specifications covering content, format, difficulty and other design features. Abstract items can reduce interference from unrelated constructs; simulation-based items can improve correspondence with real-world settings. The authors recommend Evidence-Centered Design to keep simulated scenarios focused on the intended construct rather than merely resembling existing task benchmarks.
qs: Test items should not only sufficiently reflect the targeted construct but also remain unaffected by other unrelated constructs and factors [47].
Test guidelines and item specifications provide detailed design from the macro to the micro level, ensuring that test developers adhere to precise rules when crafting items.

These test items employ real-world situations as context to increase ecological validity while leveraging techniques such as Evidence-Centered Design [64] to ensure that the target construct is measured effectively in such contexts.

kp.k: Item Response Theory enables richer and adaptive scoring
kp.d: The authors recommend Item Response Theory because it models correct-response probabilities using item parameters and estimated construct levels, unlike simple totals of equally weighted correct answers. They argue that its common measurement scale supports comparisons across changing item sets, relevant when training-data exposure necessitates test updates. Computerized Adaptive Testing can select items matched to estimated ability for more efficient, precise assessment; further diagnostic applications are presented as opportunities.
qs: This is achieved by modeling the probability of a correct response as a mathematical function of item parameters and the subject’s level of the construct [14, 65, 66].
IRT enables comparisons of AI systems even when they are evaluated in different tests with varying test formats or item sets [14, 65, 66].
Thirdly, IRT lays the groundwork for Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) [14, 65], which enables the selection of items that best match the construct level of each subject.

kp.k: Reliable scores must also predict meaningful real-world outcomes
kp.d: The validation stage distinguishes stability and consistency from whether a test measures its claimed construct. Recommended reliability checks cover repeated testing, internal consistency, equivalent test forms and rater agreement. Validity checks include factor structure, convergent and discriminant relationships, and prediction of external outcomes. The authors use better chatbot reviews and research-assistant user satisfaction as illustrative criteria, not measured improvements.
qs: Reliability refers to the consistency or stability of a test [15, 52].
Validity indicates the extent to which a test measures the construct that it claims to measure [15, 52].
Predictive validity is another form of validity that is concerned with the extent to which a score on a test predicts performance on a certain criterion measure [52].
Both construct validity and predictive validity are important since they ensure that the construct being measured by the test is related to the actual use of the AI systems in real life.

kp.k: AI populations and measurement units remain unresolved
kp.d: The authors identify uncertainty about whether different prompts, personas, fine-tuned systems or model versions constitute repeated observations of one subject or distinct subjects within a population. They tentatively propose using response variance to distinguish these cases, potentially referencing human variance, but acknowledge that thresholds and effectiveness need research. Multilevel modeling could separate prompt-, persona- and model-level effects.
qs: However, it is hard to define multiple data points collected from an AI system, which might be treated as either repeated measures or a single measure from multiple individuals.

Accordingly, we may consider an AI system under different settings as a single person generating repeated responses if the variance is small, and treat them as a population if the variance is sufficiently large.
However, this raises the question of what is considered sufficiently large.

kp.k: Prompt sensitivity complicates reliability and validity
kp.d: Open questions include whether evaluations should use typical user prompts or prompts optimized to elicit maximum performance. The authors distinguish systematic prompt effects, potentially activating an unintended construct and affecting validity, from random effects affecting reliability. They call for standardized protocols and investigation of whether unstable results warrant changing tests or improving systems themselves.
qs: Should the prompts represent how users will typically issue commands to an AI system or be carefully tuned to elicit optimal performance?
Such a systematic effect could indicate that a second construct that we did not intend to measure may have been activated, affecting the validity of the measurement.
This is a random effect that might affect the reliability of the measurement.
Currently, it is uncertain what prompts would result in systematic or random effects, and systematic and random effects may also vary between different constructs and tests.

kp.k: Human–AI comparisons need item-level fairness checks
kp.d: For assessments comparing humans with AI, or different AI systems with one another, the authors propose Differential Item Functioning to detect items that disadvantage a group after controlling for latent construct level. This is a recommended method for assessing comparability, not evidence that existing human–AI comparisons have achieved it.
qs: To ensure a fair comparison, it is important to ascertain the appropriateness of the items.
DIF offers a method using which we could examine if a test item works equally well in humans and AI systems, as well as among different AI systems.

kp.k: Human–AI teamwork requires assessment beyond standalone capabilities
kp.d: Citing productivity research, the authors anticipate an important role for human–AI collaboration while noting that evaluation of this hybrid work remains scarce. They recommend adapting psychometric approaches to collaborative performance and disentangling human and AI contributions. A previously validated human collaborative problem-solving model covering shared knowledge construction and negotiation is offered as a potential methodological resource, not a validated human–AI team assessment.
qs: Teams of humans and AI systems, where humans are assisted by AI systems or collaborate with AI systems, could be regarded as a new form of working force.

Notably, human-AI teaming depends on the capacities of both the humans and the AI system to work in a complex and dynamic context [86], therefore, it is crucial to explore methods that disentangle the contributions of different types of agents in collaboration.
These methods could help with the evaluation of human-AI teaming.

kp.k: Construct assessments could guide legal-assistant model selection
kp.d: The document’s direct legal application is prospective: the authors suggest selecting systems with evidence-relevance assessment and critical examination capabilities before substantial legal training, even if they initially lack extensive legal knowledge. They expect such systems could assist a judge after training on substantial legal datasets, potentially reducing training effort and improving resource allocation. No legal deployment results, lawyer substitution findings or cost estimates are supplied.
qs: If an AI system is capable of assessing the relevance of evidence to arguments and critically examining competing perspectives, there is a reasonable expectation that, even if it currently lacks extensive legal knowledge, it has the potential to assist a judge after being trained with substantial legal datasets.
This prospective AI selection could save a large amount of training efforts and help allocate the most valuable resources to the most high- potential AI systems.

kp.k: Evaluation should guide the entire AI development process
kp.d: Drawing an analogy with educational assessment, the authors envision construct-oriented evaluation informing objectives, system selection, training feedback, and final validation and integration. The aim is to develop capabilities and values appropriate to complex application settings rather than optimize only dataset-specific scores. This is a proposed future development process, qualified by the acknowledgment that psychometrics cannot resolve every AI evaluation problem.
qs: Similarly, the significance and role of AI evaluation should extend beyond measuring its performance after the system is trained.

Leveraging the feedback collected from the selection phase and ongoing tests, we can identify fundamental limitations (e.g., lack of critical thinking), optimize the training towards the predefined objectives, and examine whether the AI system is improving over targeted latent constructs.

While we acknowledge that psychometrics alone may not solve all issues in AI evaluation, we consider this transition crucial in the current stage and look forward to a future in which psychometrics-grounded AI evaluation in return shapes the future of human evaluation.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wang and co-authors propose that construct-oriented psychometric evaluation can improve prediction, explanation and quality assurance of general-purpose AI performance, including selection of systems for future judicial assistance.
pts.d: This is primarily a cross-domain methodological perspective, not a study of legal-service markets. The authors argue that predefined task benchmarks are insufficient for general-purpose systems facing unforeseen tasks. They propose identifying latent constructs, measuring them and validating the resulting tests. They suggest that this approach could guide model selection and training rather than merely assess completed systems. Their specific legal example is conditional: a system capable of assessing evidence and critically examining competing perspectives could have potential to assist a judge after substantial legal-data training, even without extensive initial legal knowledge. They predict that prospective selection could reduce training effort and improve resource allocation. They also anticipate an important role for human–AI collaboration and suggest adapting psychometric methods to assess teams and distinguish participants' contributions. The source does not predict lawyer displacement, changes to fees or law-firm staffing.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their proposal through established psychometric theory, cited human research and existing AI studies; the judicial-assistance example is illustrative rather than an empirically demonstrated result.
pts.d: For predictive power, the authors cite longitudinal human studies relating cognitive and personality constructs to academic and life outcomes. For explanatory power in AI, they cite Burnell and colleagues' factor analysis of 29 language models on 27 cognitive tasks, identifying reasoning, comprehension and core language modeling constructs. They cite research on prompt sensitivity and unreliable application of human personality questionnaires to AI to motivate stronger test validation. Item Response Theory and Computerized Adaptive Testing supply established methodological foundations, with cited applications to AI evaluation. The discussion of human–AI teaming invokes Noy and Zhang's 2023 experimental productivity research and a collaborative problem-solving competency model validated in human cooperative tasks. The paper supplies no new legal-assistance experiment, judicial outcome data or numerical estimate of training savings; those benefits are prospective arguments based on the proposed framework and educational analogies.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The December 2023 paper offers an undated future research and development agenda, conditional on identifying appropriate AI constructs and establishing reliable, valid measurements.
pts.d: The authors describe shortcomings of contemporary evaluation and envision future integration of psychometrics throughout AI development without specifying an adoption date. Judicial assistance is explicitly conditional on relevant reasoning capabilities and subsequent training with substantial legal datasets. More broadly, the proposed predictive benefits depend on construct validation, appropriate test design and evidence connecting scores to real-world outcomes. The authors warn against assuming that human psychological constructs or tests transfer unchanged to AI. They identify unresolved issues concerning prompt sensitivity, the definition of an AI test subject or population, and fair human–AI comparisons. They acknowledge that initial constructs may be partial or biased and require continuing refinement, and that psychometrics alone cannot resolve every evaluation problem.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed changes chiefly affect AI developers, evaluators, policymakers and human–AI teams; judges are the specific legal beneficiaries envisaged.
pts.d: Developers could use construct assessments to select promising models, allocate training resources, diagnose limitations and track improvements. Evaluators and psychometric researchers would need to build and validate AI-appropriate tests and resolve methodological questions. Researchers and policymakers are identified as needing explanations of system strengths and weaknesses to inform safety and improvement decisions. Human workers collaborating with AI would become subjects of team-level assessment rather than being assessed only separately from the system. Judges could receive assistance from appropriately selected and legally trained AI systems. Users and the public are intended beneficiaries of evaluations that better connect measured capabilities to real-world performance and responsible deployment. The paper does not distinguish law-firm types, client segments or legal-provider business models.
